headline_marked: No [[enforced disappearances or extrajudicial killings]] in last 6 months: Home Minister
headline: No enforced disappearances or extrajudicial killings in last 6 months: Home Minister
summary: Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed asserts no political persecution has occurred since the current government took office, while discussing a new draft law to prevent disappearances.
details: Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed stated on Saturday that no one in Bangladesh has been subjected to enforced disappearance, extrajudicial killing, or political persecution since the current government took office six months ago.

The remarks were made during a panel discussion organized by Mayer Daak at the National Museum auditorium in Shahbagh, held on the eve of the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances.

Addressing the disappearance of Miraj Sheikh, the minister said an independent investigation found no political motive, suggesting the incident might be linked to conflicts among robber groups in the Sundarbans.
Salahuddin discussed the draft Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Act 2026, stating the law aims to ensure victims can approach courts for justice and redress.
The proposed law includes definitions of disappearance, investigation procedures, and punishments, with the death penalty as the maximum sentence.
It also provides for compensation and ensures that heirs receive property rights to support their families if a disappeared person does not return.
Human rights activist Nur Khan Liton challenged these claims, alleging that eyewitness accounts and digital data indicate law enforcement involvement in Miraj Sheikh's disappearance.
Liton demanded a transparent probe into the roles of the police and Coast Guard, emphasizing that an independent investigation is paramount for the new law to be effective.
caption:
No enforced disappearances or extrajudicial killings in the last 6 months, claims Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed.

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed stated on Saturday that no one in Bangladesh has been subjected to enforced disappearance, extrajudicial killing, or political persecution since the current government took office six months ago.

The remarks were made during a panel discussion organized by Mayer Daak at the National Museum auditorium in Shahbagh, held on the eve of the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances.

Addressing the disappearance of Miraj Sheikh, the minister said an independent investigation found no political motive, suggesting the incident might be linked to conflicts among robber groups in the Sundarbans.

Salahuddin discussed the draft Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Act 2026, stating the law aims to ensure victims can approach courts for justice and redress.

The proposed law includes definitions of disappearance, investigation procedures, and punishments, with the death penalty as the maximum sentence.

It also provides for compensation and ensures that heirs receive property rights to support their families if a disappeared person does not return.

Human rights activist Nur Khan Liton challenged these claims, alleging that eyewitness accounts and digital data indicate law enforcement involvement in Miraj Sheikh's disappearance.

Liton demanded a transparent probe into the roles of the police and Coast Guard, emphasizing that an independent investigation is paramount for the new law to be effective.

headline_marked: Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council [[claims police cover-up in Rangpur killings]]
headline: Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council claims police cover-up in Rangpur killings
summary: The organization held a human chain at the National Press Club to demand a judicial probe into the murder of four family members, including a retired teacher.
details: The Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council has alleged that a 'special circle' murdered four members of a family in Rangpur for sinister motives. The victims included Ganapati Chakraborty, a retired teacher of Rangpur Zilla School, and three other family members.

Leaders of the organization held a human chain and a protest march in front of the National Press Club on Saturday morning. They claimed that police efforts are underway to hide the actual events or divert the investigation.

The Council stated that the police narrative regarding the killings is not believable. They argued that such incidents create panic among minorities nationwide and may provoke them to leave the country.

The organization has demanded an immediate statement from the government in Parliament and a judicial inquiry to identify the real culprits. They called for exemplary punishment for those responsible.
In a separate press release, the Council highlighted ongoing communal violence in the country. They cited reports of 41 communal incidents in July alone, including 6 killings and 2 rapes.
The report further detailed 10 cases of idol desecration and looting in temples, 5 attacks on ethnic minorities, and 10 attacks on homes and businesses, including 2 cases of forced land grabbing.
